articles.body_html:
My smart light bulb tried to mine crypto last Tuesday.

Not a joke. Not a metaphor.

I have a cheap Tuya bulb I bought from for $12.99 in 2023. "Smart Life" app, WiFi enabled, 16 million colors, works with Alexa. I put it in my closet so I could say "closet on" and feel like I'm in .

At 3:17 AM, my network monitor woke me up. Not an alarm — just a little red dot on my Grafana dashboard. My closet bulb had uploaded 400MB of data to an IP address in Shenzhen and was now holding a persistent outbound connection on port 3333. Port 3333 is not for turning on lights. Port 3333 is for Monero mining pools.

I unplugged it. I took it apart. Inside was an ESP8266 clone, 2MB of flash, firmware from 2019 with a hardcoded Telnet password: admin:admin. And a little bonus binary called xmr_mini hidden in a partition that shouldn't exist.

That bulb was $13. It had no business having enough brains to betray me, but it did. And it's not alone. Your house is full of them.

Welcome to the Internet of Shit.

The Lie We All Bought

The IoT pitch was beautiful: everything connected, everything smart, everything effortless.

The reality is this: a $400 billion industry built on the cheapest possible chips, running the oldest possible Linux kernels, written by the lowest bidder, shipped with default credentials that haven't changed since 2008.

Here's the math that kills you:

A company wants to sell a smart plug for $9.99.

  • The ESP8266 chip costs $0.89
  • The relay costs $0.40
  • The plastic costs $0.30
  • The profit margin needs to be $4

Where do you think they cut costs? Security audits? Code review? A firmware update server?

No. They cut everything.

They take the SDK example code from Espressif that says // TODO: CHANGE DEFAULT PASSWORD, they don't change the default password, they compile it, and they ship 500,000 units.

I've dumped firmware from 23 different IoT devices in the last year. Light bulbs, cameras, doorbells, pet feeders, a smart toaster — yes, a toaster that can run Doom and also get botnetted.

Here is what I find, every single time:

1. Telnet or SSH open with root:root or admin:admin
In 2026. After Mirai. After 8 years of us screaming about Mirai.

2. A web server running as root from 2016
With a CVE list longer than my grocery list. No update mechanism. Ever.

3. Hardcoded MQTT credentials
One username and password for every device they ever sold. mqtt_user: TuyaSmart123! — I found that in 4 different brands.

4. Cloud buckets with no auth
Your camera footage, your voice clips, your WiFi password — sitting in an open S3 bucket because the intern left public: true in the config.

This isn't a bug. This is the business model.

My Living Room Botnet Census

I got angry after the light bulb thing, so I did what any normal person does: I turned my apartment into a surveillance state for my own devices.

I took that $26 GL.iNet Mango router — the little yellow travel router everyone buys for hotel WiFi — and I made it my border guard.

I flashed it with OpenWrt. Put it between my modem and my real router. Installed:

  • Pi-hole to DNS-blackhole every ad, tracker, and telemetry domain
  • AdGuard Home as backup
  • Suricata in IDS mode to watch what my devices actually say

Then I let it run for 7 days. I didn't block anything. I just watched.

Here is what my "smart" home does when I'm not looking:

My $35 Wyze camera: Pings wyze-log.s3.amazonaws.com every 30 seconds, even when I have "record only on motion" turned off. Uploaded 2.1GB in a week. Of what? I'm not recording 2.1GB of my living room wall.

My smart TV (TCL ): At 2am every night, it resolves 47 different ad domains. It tried to reach doubleclick.net 14,000 times in 7 days. Fourteen thousand. It also sends my WiFi SSID and a list of nearby SSIDs to Roku every 6 hours. Why does Roku need to know my neighbor's WiFi name?

My robot vacuum: Sent a compressed map of my apartment — literally a floorplan of where my bed is — to a server in Singapore. The privacy policy says "to improve cleaning." My bed doesn't need to be in Singapore.

My wife's smart toothbrush: Yes, this exists. It sends brush time, pressure, and location to . 19 times a day.

The worst offender? A $19 smart plug from a brand that doesn't exist anymore. It tried to SSH into my NAS. My own plug tried to brute force my own NAS on my local network. Because its firmware had Mirai's old dictionary baked in and it scans /24s automatically.

We put computers that actively attack other computers inside our houses and then act surprised when they do.

Why Your Router is Lying to You

Your ISP router is not a router. It's a plastic box designed to blink green so you stop calling tech support.

It does NAT. It does WiFi badly. It does not inspect traffic. It does not tell you that your light bulb is mining Monero. It will never tell you.

You need a watchtower.

This is why I tell everyone to build a $20 SOC — Security Operations Center. It sounds insane. SOCs are for enterprises with 6 monitors and cold brew on tap. But a $20 SOC is just a tiny Linux box that sits and judges all your other boxes.

The Mango costs $20-26 on Amazon. Total build with a USB stick for logs is under $30. It draws 2 watts. It has no subscription. It will outlive your smart fridge.

What it gives you:

  • Visibility. For the first time, you see that your bulb is talking to 45.76.123.89 at 3am. That alone is worth it.
  • Blocking at the root. Pi-hole kills ads, trackers, and 80% of malware C2 domains before they even leave your house. Your TV gets dumber — which is good. Dumb TVs can't snitch.
  • Receipts. When that bulb gets popped, you have logs. When you call the manufacturer and they say "impossible," you send them a pcap. They shut up very fast.

The second part of my setup is even more paranoid: an offline box.

I have a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W — $35 if you're lucky — running a local LLM completely offline. No WiFi, no cloud. I call it the Blackbox. I feed it suspicious firmware dumps, weird log lines, long ToS documents I don't want to upload to ChatGPT. It summarizes, it finds hardcoded creds, it writes abuse emails. Nothing ever leaves my apartment.

When you're dissecting a light bulb that tried to rob you, you don't want to paste its private key into someone else's cloud.

The Fix Isn't What You Think

People want me to say "don't buy smart devices." That's not realistic. I'm not going to hand-wash dishes because my dishwasher has WiFi.

The fix is hostile architecture. Treat every IoT device like it's already compromised, because statistically, it is.

My rules now:

1. VLAN or it didn't happen. All IoT shit goes on its own WiFi network that can't talk to my laptops, NAS, or phones. The Mango makes this 3 clicks. Your main router probably doesn't. That's why you need the Mango.

2. No internet unless it proves it needs it. My light bulbs don't need internet to turn on. I block their internet at DNS level. If they stop working, good — I return them and buy ones that work locally with Home Assistant or ESPHome. If a light bulb requires the cloud to turn on, it's not a light bulb, it's a subscription to light.

3. Flash or trash. If a device runs ESP8266/ESP32, I flash it with Tasmota or ESPHome immediately. Open firmware, local control, no cloud, no mystery binaries. It takes 10 minutes and it turns a spy into a tool. If I can't flash it, I don't buy it.

4. Assume default passwords. First thing I do with any new device: nmap it. nmap -p 23,22,80,8080 <its IP>. If Telnet is open, I try admin/admin, root/root, admin/password. It works 60% of the time. I then change it or brick it.

5. Log everything for 7 days. When you get a new device, put it in the watchtower and just watch. If it phones home 14,000 times, you know.

The IoT industry will not fix itself. There is no incentive. A $13 bulb that is secure costs $15. And $15 loses to $13 on Amazon every time. Security is invisible until it fails, and failure is externalized onto you.

The only person who can secure your house is you. And it doesn't take a $10,000 rack. It takes $26, a USB stick, and the willingness to accept that your smart home is actually a very dumb botnet that you happen to live in.

My closet light is now running ESPHome. It turns on. It turns off. It doesn't mine crypto. It doesn't talk to Shenzhen. It took me 20 minutes to flash.

It is the only smart device in my house I trust.

The rest are in jail.

Want to build the same jail I use?

This is the exact defensive stack from this story — the parts lists, flash commands, Pi-hole blocklists, and Suricata rules I use so my own light bulbs can't betray me:

The $20 SOC: Build a Tiny Defensive Network Monitor — The Mango build, step-by-step. How to put a Pi-hole + IDS between your modem and your whole house, VLAN your IoT, and finally see what your TV does at 2am. My live configs and power measurements inside: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/20dollarsoxc

BUILD THE BLACKBOX: An Offline AI Field Terminal That Works When Nothing Else Does — The Pi Zero that runs Phi-3/Gemma locally with no cloud. I use it to dissect firmware, parse logs, and draft abuse reports without ever sending your home data to OpenAI: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/blackbox-offline-ai

articles.body_html:
It started with a text message at 11:47 PM.

Your USPS package could not be delivered. Please confirm address within 12 hours: usps-resolve-helpdesk[.]com/track

I don't have a USPS package coming. I know it's a scam. You know it's a scam. My mom would click it.

I usually delete these. This time I didn't. I was bored, I was wired on bad coffee, and I had a fresh Kali VM open.

I decided to click back.

Hour 0: Building The Cage

Rule #1 if you're going to poke scammers: never do it from your real life.

I spun up what I call my cage. It's not fancy:

  • A Mullvad VPN exit in another state
  • A Firefox profile that has never logged into anything real, running in a VM with no access to my files
  • A burner email from SimpleLogin, a Google Voice number that forwards to nowhere
  • Burp Suite open, recording everything

I clicked.

The site was a perfect clone of USPS. Good CSS, good logo, even the tracking animation. It asked for my address and a $1.45 redelivery fee. Classic.

I put in fake data. 123 Fuckyou Lane, Charlotte NC. The burner email. And a fake card number from Stripe's test card list: 4242 4242 4242 4242. Any payment form that accepts that without a Stripe test mode is not talking to Stripe. It's talking directly to a Telegram bot or a panel.

It accepted it. Of course it did.

Then it said "Payment Failed - Try Another Card." And it asked again.

That's the tell. They don't want $1.45. They want you to burn through 2-3 real cards trying. Each attempt is logged.

I checked the page source. The form action was posting to https:// usps-resolve-helpdesk[.]com/api/verify.php. Not USPS. Obvious. But inside that JS file was something less obvious:
A hardcoded Telegram bot token. In client-side JavaScript.

Amateur hour. Or they just don't care because they burn domains every 48 hours anyway.

I saved the token. I didn't touch the Telegram API yet — that's crossing a line from OSINT into unauthorized access. But I now had a thread to pull.

Hour 8: Day 1 - Who Are You?

I ran the domain.

Registered 2 days ago on Namecheap with privacy guard. Hosted on a cheap VPS in Moscow, ASN 203...something. Cloudflare in front of it.

But the phishing kit itself had left metadata. The favicon was /favicon.ico?v=usps2024 — same string I found in 11 other domains on URLScan.io. Same kit author.

I pivoted on URLScan. Found 3 other live clones:

  • dhl-express-fix[.]com
  • tolls-ezpass-pay[.]com
  • chase-secure-alert[.]com

Same kit, same Telegram exfil structure, same bad opsec.

The scammer was running multiple campaigns off the same infrastructure. This wasn't a lone kid. This was a small operation.

I fed the burner email I used into HaveIBeenPwned, Dehashed, IntelX. Nothing. But the phone number I gave them? Within 4 hours I got a call.

Indian accent, call center noise in background. "Hello, this is USPS, we are calling about your package, your card did not work..."

I answered with a voice changer. "Oh thank god, yeah my card..."

He wanted me to read the card number over the phone. I gave him another fake one, slowly. He typed it. I heard him swear in Hindi when his own checker said invalid.

Then he got angry. "Madam, why you are wasting my time?"

That was the first time it got personal. He knew. He'd flagged me as a time-waster. Most people hang up here.

I apologized and said I was confused. He softened, went back to script. He asked for my real name to "verify the address."

I said "Lusynth." He paused. "What kind of name is that?"

Now it was really personal.

Hour 24: Day 2 - The Flip

I stopped playing victim and started playing bigger fish.

I sent a message to the burner number from another burner: "Hey bro, your USPS panel is showing token in source. You should fix. Also your Cloudflare is leaking origin IP via email headers when you send the smishing."

I was bluffing on the second part. But it's true 70% of the time.

He replied in 11 minutes: "who is this"

I said: "I buy logs. You have US logs? I saw your domain on Telegram. I want to buy."

This is how the ecosystem works. The kid who smishes is often not the guy who cashes out. He sells the "logs" — fullz — to someone else for $5-$15 each.

He sent me a Telegram handle. Not his personal — a business account with 2,300 subscribers. @usps_logs_live. Bio: "Fresh USPS/DHL/Chase - $8 per log - bulk - escrow"

Bingo. This was his storefront.

I joined with a sock puppet Telegram account. His channel had screenshots of "successful logs" — credit cards with last 4, bank names, victims' zips. One was from Charlotte. 28262. My zip code.

That one hit weird. Someone 10 minutes from me got hit by this exact guy and now their card is in his inventory.

I scraped the channel history with a Telegram export. 4 months of posts. I found patterns:

  • He posted mostly 9am - 6pm IST. So India timezone.
  • He always used the same Bitcoin address for escrow.
  • He reused the same username on a blackhat forum from 2023: desi_hustler_99.

I took that username and ran it through Sherlock, WhatsMyName. Found a GitHub. Found a now-deleted YouTube channel that taught "ethical hacking" with the same voice from the phone call.

He was 19. From his GitHub commits, learning Python from a course. His real name was in a commit email.

I'm not going to share it. That's doxxing and it's not the point. The point is, for 5 hours I had turned a random smishing text into a whole person.

And I felt sick.

Not because he was a mastermind. Because he wasn't. He was a kid who learned requests library 6 months ago and realized he could make more in a day scamming than his dad makes in a month. And he was good at it enough to hurt real people near me.

Hour 52: Day 3 - Shutting It Down Without Becoming Him

This is where most "I hacked the scammer" stories turn into revenge porn. They delete his files, they swat him, they leak his data. That's not justice, that's just becoming a different kind of criminal and getting your Medium account banned.

What actually hurts these operations is boring, unsexy, defensive work.

Here's what I did:

1. Killed the infrastructure. I reported the origin IP and domains to Cloudflare Abuse, Namecheap, and the host's abuse@ with full logs, headers, and the Telegram bot token. I also reported the Telegram bot to @botfather and the channel to Telegram abuse. Cloudflare dropped him in 6 hours. Namecheap suspended the domain in 12. His Telegram bot stopped responding by hour 60. His business is gone for that week.

2. Poisoned his logs. All those fake cards I fed him? I kept feeding them. 40 fake submissions over 72 hours from different fake personas via a simple Python script + Selenium. Every fake log he tries to sell now makes him look like a scammer to other scammers. His reputation on his own channel tanked. People started calling him rippper in comments.

3. Protected my own perimeter. I took that Charlotte victim zip as a warning. I rebuilt my home network trap. This is where my real work lives.

I don't use a normal router anymore. I use a little $26 travel router that runs OpenWrt — the GL Mango. I flashed it and put it between my modem and everything else. It runs Pi-hole to kill tracking and ad domains, and a tiny IDS that logs whenever an IoT device talks to a weird IP at 3am. It has saved me twice.

And I have a second box — a Pi Zero that runs a fully offline LLM. No cloud, no API keys. I use it to parse logs, summarize abuse reports, and draft the emails to hosting providers without ever sending victim data to OpenAI. When you do this kind of work, the last thing you want is to leak a victim's PII into someone else's training set.

What 72 Hours Actually Taught Me

Scammers aren't hackers. They're businessmen with bad code. Their opsec is terrible. They reuse passwords, they leave tokens in JS, they use the same BTC address. You don't need to be a 0-day god to beat them. You need to be patient and systematic.

The infrastructure is the product. Taking down one domain does nothing. Taking down his Telegram bot, his Cloudflare front, and poisoning his reputation does. Attack the business model, not the kid.

It will feel personal, and that's the trap. When you hear someone from your own city got hit, when the guy mocks your name, you want revenge. Revenge makes you sloppy and makes you cross lines that will get you in trouble. Document, report, sinkhole. Don't hack back.

Your family is the real attack surface. That USPS text wasn't aimed at me. It was aimed at my mom, your mom, anyone who is tired and expects a package. The best defense isn't your fancy EDR. It's a 10-minute conversation with your family: "The USPS will never text you for $1.45. If you're unsure, forward it to me."

I didn't save the world in 72 hours. I probably cost one 19-year-old about $400 in lost sales and a weekend of rebuilding his kit. He'll be back next week with a new domain.

But one domain gone means maybe 30 fewer people in 28262 get that text tonight. That's enough for me.

Don't try to be a hero. Be a speed bump.

Want the build notes for the defensive setup I used in this story?

I keep all the actual how-to stuff — the firmware, wiring, flash commands, blocklists, and offline AI setup — off Medium and in two guides I update constantly:

The $20 SOC: Build a Tiny Defensive Network Monitor — How I turned that GL.iNet Mango into a full Pi-hole + IDS + logging box that catches exactly this kind of IoT exfil and smishing infra. Parts list, flash steps, my configs: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/20dollarsoxc

BUILD THE BLACKBOX: An Offline AI Field Terminal That Works When Nothing Else Does — The Pi Zero box that runs a local LLM with no internet, so you can analyze sketchy logs and write abuse reports without leaking anything to the cloud: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/blackbox-offline-ai

articles.title: Component Architecture: Co-location, Composition, and Separation of Concerns, Different soups...
articles.description: One thing I think frontend engineers need to be more deliberate about is how we apply software design...
articles.body_html:
One thing I think frontend engineers need to be more deliberate about is how we apply software design principles when building component-based applications.

There is a tendency to treat co-location, separation of concerns, reusability, and Atomic Design as though they all mean the same thing: breaking code into smaller pieces and organizing those pieces into folders. They do not. Each principle addresses a different problem, and misunderstanding the distinction can lead to abstractions that look reusable on the surface but become increasingly difficult to maintain.

1. Co-location is about proximity, not combining everything into one component

Co-location means keeping code close to the part of the application it relates to. The underlying idea is that code that changes together should generally be located together.

For example, suppose a feature has a component, its validation schema, feature-specific hooks, helper functions, and tests. Keeping those things within the feature's module makes it easier to understand, modify, and maintain that feature without navigating an unrelated collection of global folders.

But co-location does not mean combining all those responsibilities into one component or file.

Consider a password input that is used only by an authentication feature. It makes sense to keep its implementation close to the authentication feature while it remains specific to that context. If it eventually becomes useful across multiple features, we can extract it into a shared UI module.

The important distinction is that co-location determines where code belongs; separation of concerns determines what responsibilities that code should have.

These principles complement each other. They do not compete.

2. Separation of concerns is about responsibility

Separation of concerns means dividing a system into units with clearly defined responsibilities. A component should have a coherent purpose and a contract that makes its behavior understandable.

Consider a generic input component. Its responsibility might include rendering a native input, forwarding standard input attributes, supporting accessibility, and applying the design system's styling.

Now imagine extending that same component to handle all of the following:

  • Standard text inputs.
  • Password inputs with visibility toggles.
  • OTP inputs with multiple digit slots.
  • Grouped inputs with prefixes, suffixes, or multiple fields.
  • Input-specific validation, formatting, keyboard navigation, and specialized error handling.

We could expose a type prop and several additional flags, then use conditional statements to decide which implementation to render.

That might appear efficient because everything is available through one component. However, the component is gradually taking responsibility for several different interaction patterns, each with its own state, behavior, accessibility requirements, and testing needs.

The problem is not simply that the file has become large. The deeper problem is that its interface and implementation are now responsible for too many distinct concerns.

A change to OTP navigation should not require us to reason about password visibility. A change to password visibility should not risk breaking the behavior of an ordinary text field.

A shared component should provide a stable foundation, not become a container for every component that happens to involve an input.

3. Atomic Design helps us reason about the level of abstraction

Atomic Design provides a useful vocabulary for organizing interfaces into atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.

A basic input can be treated as an atom: a foundational UI primitive. A form field combining a label, input, and error message can be treated as a molecule. A larger form section combining several fields, validation feedback, and submission controls might be an organism, depending on its scope and complexity.

However, Atomic Design is a mental model, not a rigid classification system. The correct level of abstraction depends on what a component does, what it depends on, and how it is used.

For example:

  • Input: A generic, reusable primitive with a clearly defined contract.
  • PasswordInput: A specialized component that composes the generic input with password-specific behavior, such as a visibility toggle.
  • OTPInput: A specialized component that manages multiple digit positions, focus movement, and keyboard interactions.
  • InputGroup: A composition that combines an input with adjacent elements, such as a prefix, suffix, or action.
  • FormField: A higher-level composition that associates a control with its label, description, and validation feedback.

These are not necessarily five atoms. They operate at different levels of abstraction.

The goal is not to create a separate component for every possible variation. The goal is to ensure that each abstraction represents a coherent responsibility and that higher-level components build on lower-level primitives rather than forcing every behavior into one primitive.

4. Composition is how we build specialized behavior without bloating foundational components

Composition allows us to build complex interfaces by combining smaller components with well-defined responsibilities.

Instead of making the generic Input component understand every possible input pattern, we can build specialized components around it.

For example:

function PasswordInput(props: InputProps) {
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div className="password-input">
      <Input
        {...props}
        type={visible ? "text" : "password"}
      />

      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => setVisible((value) => !value)}
        aria-label={visible ? "Hide password" : "Show password"}
      >
        {visible ? <EyeOff /> : <Eye />}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

This is a simplified illustration, but it demonstrates the architectural distinction: the generic input remains responsible for rendering an input, while the password component owns the additional password-specific interaction.

The OTP input can have its own implementation for digit management, focus movement, and keyboard behavior. It may reuse the same design tokens, styling conventions, and lower-level primitives without forcing the generic input to implement OTP-specific logic.

Likewise, an input group can compose a generic input with prefixes, suffixes, or action buttons.

The objective is not to eliminate conditional rendering. Conditional rendering is perfectly reasonable when it expresses a genuine variation within a component's responsibility. The problem arises when a component becomes a large conditional dispatcher for unrelated behaviors.

Composition gives us a way to reuse implementation without coupling every consumer to every other use case.

React supports this through component nesting, children, and explicit props. A component can provide a structural foundation while allowing its consumer to determine what content or specialized component belongs inside it.

5. Reusability does not mean putting every use case behind one API

A common architectural mistake is assuming that if two components share a visual element, they should necessarily be represented by one highly configurable component.

But visual similarity does not always imply behavioral similarity.

A password input, an OTP input, and a grouped input all involve inputs, but their interaction models differ substantially. Their shared foundation does not justify merging their responsibilities.

A better approach is to reuse at the appropriate level:

  • Reuse design tokens for consistent spacing, typography, colors, and sizing.
  • Reuse generic primitives for common rendering and styling.
  • Compose specialized components from those primitives where it makes sense.
  • Keep feature-specific behavior within the feature that owns it.
  • Promote a feature-specific abstraction into a shared module when there is a genuine need for broader reuse.

This also avoids premature abstraction. A component does not need to become globally available simply because it has been written once. Reuse should emerge from a clear contract and a real need, rather than from the desire to eliminate every instance of duplication.

6. Component boundaries and code splitting are related, but they are not the same thing

There is another important distinction here.

Keeping unrelated implementations together can make architectural boundaries harder to understand and maintain. It can also contribute to unnecessarily large bundles when the module dependency graph causes code to be included together.

However, putting components in separate files does not automatically guarantee code splitting. Modern bundlers determine chunks from the import graph, build configuration, and dynamic import boundaries.

If an OTP implementation is only needed on a particular route, a deliberate dynamic import or lazy-loaded feature boundary may allow that code to be loaded separately. Merely extracting OTPInput into its own file does not guarantee this result.

The architectural benefit of separation is that it gives us clearer units of responsibility and makes independent loading, testing, and evolution easier to reason about. The bundler still needs the appropriate module boundaries to produce the desired output.

We should avoid confusing a good component architecture with an automatic performance optimization.

7. Why this matters even more in the AI era

AI can generate components, refactor files, create abstractions, and reproduce patterns very quickly. But generating code that works is not the same as designing a system that remains maintainable as it grows.

If we ask an AI tool to build a reusable input component without defining the intended boundaries, it may produce a single component with a long list of props, conditional branches, and flags to accommodate every foreseeable use case.

That implementation may work. It may even look elegant in a small example. But it can introduce hidden coupling, unclear contracts, and unnecessary complexity as more requirements are added.

The problem is not that AI inherently produces poor architecture. It is that AI needs architectural constraints and evaluation criteria, just as a human engineer does. Without them, local convenience can take precedence over the long-term structure of the application.

This is where engineering principles become more valuable, not less.

A design system should do more than standardize colors, spacing, typography, and component appearance. It should also establish rules for component responsibility, composition, dependency direction, state ownership, and reuse.

For example, a design system should make the following expectations explicit:

  • Foundational UI primitives should remain focused on their core responsibilities.
  • Specialized interactions should be composed from existing primitives where appropriate.
  • Feature-specific logic should remain close to the feature that owns it.
  • Shared components should expose clear, strongly typed contracts.
  • New abstractions should be introduced when they address a real need, not merely to make code appear more reusable.
  • Generated code should be reviewed for architectural fit, not only whether it renders correctly.

These rules give an AI coding tool a set of constraints against which to evaluate its own implementation. They also make code review more objective because the team can assess whether the implementation follows an agreed architectural model rather than relying solely on individual preferences.

Conclusion

Good component architecture shouldn't be about creating the smallest possible components or the fewest possible files. It should be about finding the right boundaries between responsibilities.

Co-location tells us where related code should live. Separation of concerns tells us which responsibilities should remain distinct. Atomic Design gives us a vocabulary for understanding levels of UI abstraction. Composition gives us a mechanism for building richer interfaces from focused components.

When these principles are applied together, a design system becomes more than a collection of reusable UI elements. It becomes an architectural contract that helps developers and AI tools build software that can evolve without accumulating unnecessary complexity.

articles.title: C = 1.25 is a tolerance, not a constant: the load-tail law behind MoE token dropping
articles.description: A capacity factor and a target drop rate are the same information in two forms, and the folk constant names only one of them. The exact drop functional, the ceiling balancing cannot reach, which tokens actually get dropped, and one command that reproduces every number.
articles.body_html:
Every sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer has a number in it that nobody derived. You need a static shape for the kernel, so each expert gets a budget c = C · topk · T / E, and C — the capacity factor — arrives as folklore: 1.25 from Switch Transformer, 2.0 from GShard. Those values were chosen at a particular expert count, batch size and load, and then re-used across expert counts from 8 to 2048 and across both training and serving.

The question worth asking is what C = 1.25 means. It turns out it means a tolerance, and the tolerance is one you do not want at decode time.

The drop rate is an exact function, so this is arithmetic rather than vibes

Under top-k routing with independent per-token decisions, expert e receives N_e ~ Bin(T, q_e) tokens, where q_e = k · p_e and p is the router's distribution. By linearity of expectation, the expected dropped-token rate depends only on the marginals:

D(C) = (1/T) Σ_e E[(N_e − c)+],      c = C · k · T / E = C · µ,   µ := k·T/E

Nothing about the joint routing pattern beyond the marginals enters. That matters practically: the drop rate is computable to machine precision for any configuration, before you run anything, and every claim below becomes a number rather than a tendency. µ — the per-expert mean load — is the axis everything turns on.

Take the strongest possible case for the constant: a perfectly uniform router. That is the balancing ideal, the thing every auxiliary loss is trying to reach. Here is what it needs, at a drop tolerance of 1e-6, for E = 64:

µ (mean load/expert) C_min for D < 1e-6 dropped at C = 1.25
1 7.97 29.89 %
2 5.43 18.77 %
4 3.80 10.10 %
8 2.82 5.23 %
16 2.19 2.24 %
128 1.36 0.01 %

Read the last column twice. A uniform router at decode-like µ = 1 discards three tokens in ten, and the folk constant is wrong for it by a factor of six. Every cell with µ ≤ 16 needs C > 2. At training load (µ = 128) the same constant is fine — 8.29e-05 drops. Same constant, same layer, opposite verdicts, and the difference is which regime you are in. Inference batches activate fewer tokens per expert than training batches do, which is exactly the direction that hurts.

Half of the required capacity is not a router property

C_min decomposes into two terms: an imbalance term (how far the router's own maximum load sits above uniform) and a finite-sample max-load term (how far a finite batch's maximum count sits above its mean). Balancing objectives act on the first. The second is a property of sampling.

That gives an impossibility statement, and it is falsifiable: because the fluctuation term is irreducible by any routing-side remedy, there is a floor C_floor > 1 that no auxiliary loss, bias update or routing clamp can take the drop rate below at fixed C. Measured at E = 16, T = 8192:

  • C_floor = 1.16354, and the decomposition says why — imbalance 1.0, noise 0.10407.
  • Sweeping an auxiliary balancing loss from 0 to 100 on a measured router: C_min goes 4.183 → 3.087 → 1.570 → 1.387 → 1.370 → 1.467 (the last step is the loss starting to cost).

So balancing buys a great deal and then stops, at 1.37 against a floor of 1.1635. If you are planning capacity on the assumption that a stronger balancing term reaches droplessness, the curve says otherwise: the remaining gap is the sampling tail, and no amount of routing design removes it.

The inversion: a capacity factor and a target drop rate are the same information

This is the part I would put in front of anyone who inherits a constant. Invert the law and C = 1.25 encodes an implicit tolerance of about 1e-2. The constant is not wrong. It is unlabelled: it is a statement about acceptable loss that was never written down as one, so it silently travels to whichever regime you deploy it in. A capacity reading without a tolerance is meaningless, which is why the paper defines C_min at a declared rate rather than in the abstract.

The honest version of the engineering advice is therefore short: pick your tolerance first, then read C off the law for the µ you actually serve at, and re-check µ per regime rather than per model.

Which tokens get dropped is not random either

Under the standard first-come dispatch, the dropped set is position-biased — 0.00 % of drops in the first decile of arrivals against 19.41 % in the last — and hot-expert concentrated, at 7–17× the uniform null. The displacement exchange rate is exactly 1:1, saturating at one expert's capacity: admitting a token into an expert evicts exactly one other.

That last fact is why this stopped being a pure efficiency question. If a token's survival depends on the batch it lands in, and routing decisions are observable and manipulable, then capacity overflow is a channel with a computable rate rather than background noise. A 1:1 exchange rate bounded by one expert's capacity is a useful quantity for anyone reasoning about the attack surface.

Placing the field's configurations on the curve

Eight published production configurations land on the law. Some of them (where the paper's config is known or reconstructible):

configuration E topk C_min at µ = 8 C_min at µ = 256
Switch Transformer (C=1.25) 2048 1 2.486 1.238
GShard (C=2.0) 2048 2 2.538 1.248
Mixtral 8x7B 8 2 1.597 1.217
DeepSeek-V3 (no-drop policy) 256 8 2.208 1.263

The pattern is the same one the uniform table showed: inside the constant's validity region at training load, outside it at decode load, with the margin depending on µ and not on the model. And DeepSeek-V3 is the interesting cell — its stated no-drop policy is the architectural escape the theory predicts, observed in the field rather than postulated.

One command, and what "reproduce" is allowed to mean

Everything above comes from one script, and I ran it before writing this:

bash reproduce.sh                    # expected final line: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN
REPRODUCE_QUICK=1 bash reproduce.sh  # skips only claim 1; ≈ 9 min

My run, from an origin/main archive export on CPython 3.9.6 / numpy 2.0.2: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN, in quick mode — so claim 1's second pass printed SKIP rather than OK, and the other five claims ran for real. The full mode is the same command without the variable, about 17 minutes. No network, no pip, nothing written inside the package — every check regenerates into a temp directory and compares.

The design detail I would steal is in how the claims are separated. "Reproduce" is not one property:

  1. the instrument suite is deterministic — two full runs byte-identical in both the artefact and the log;
  2. the committed artefact is what the code produces (regenerated and cmp-ed);
  3. the committed figures are views of that artefact (all four PNGs re-rendered byte-identical, hashes computed rather than typed);
  4. the committed manuscript equals what the pipeline builds;
  5. citation coverage and the generated citation report regenerate byte-identically;
  6. the manuscript's decisive numbers reappear from the code's own stdout.

Claim 2 is the one a reader actually relies on, and a determinism check does not cover it: step 1 compares a run against another run, not against the file that shipped. Both run, and each reports the count it read. In my run: canonical_results.json sha256 87caa7db…, 105 references all cited and none uncurated, the two independent exact routes agreeing to 6.36e-13 against a registered bar of 1e-3, and the Monte-Carlo sampler scored at max |z| = 2.17 over 5 cells. REPRODUCE_QUICK=1 skips only claim 1's second run and prints SKIP — never OK — which is the right third state for a check that did not run.

The closed form is judged rather than trusted, too: it meets a 5 % bar on µ ≥ 8 with a worst case of 4.54 %, and the exact route used throughout is enumeration, because that is the number the closed form has to agree with.

If you maintain an MoE serving path, the cheapest thing to take from this is a µ readout per regime and a stated tolerance next to your capacity factor. If the two disagree, the constant is not the problem — the missing label is.

This is paper #118 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is The Capacity Factor Is Not a Constant: A Load-Tail Law for Token Dropping in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts; the source, the instruments and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-118 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a capacity factor in production that was calibrated on training-load batches and is applied to decode-load batches, the frontier table for your E is the kind of data this line of work is short of.

articles.title: The Ariadne Thread: Why AI Fails to Follow the Path You Define
